analysis.one_liner: Limits lawsuits against small-aircraft manufacturers after crashes by preempting state liability rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred many lawsuits against small-plane makers, drew 26 bipartisan Senate cosponsors and a committee hearing but never got a vote, dying when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced state product-liability law for accidents involving small, private aircraft. It would have set a 20-year cutoff running from when an aircraft or part was delivered, after which victims generally could not sue the manufacturer, cut the filing window after a crash to two years, restrict punitive damages, and move most cases from state to federal court. The premise was that the threat of lawsuits over decades-old planes was making small-aircraft manufacturing and its insurance too costly to sustain. The bill was introduced by Sen. Nancy Kassebaum of Kansas, a state where Cessna and Beechcraft are based, and gained 26 cosponsors. The Senate Commerce Committee held one hearing in September 1991 but never voted it out, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: General aviation manufacturers — companies that build small private planes, propellers, and replacement parts — and their liability insurers. By setting a 20-year cutoff measured from delivery and a two-year filing window after an accident, the bill would have barred most suits over older aircraft, capping an industry's largest recurring legal cost. Plaintiffs' ability to win punitive damages would also have been narrowed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that it supersedes state laws on liability for general aviation accidents, replacing a patchwork of state rules with one federal standard favorable to manufacturers.

It sets a limitation period of 20 years from delivery of the aircraft or a harm-causing part, after which a civil suit against the manufacturer generally cannot be brought — effectively shutting out claims about planes built decades earlier.
It sets a two-year limitation period for actions arising out of a general aviation accident, a tight window for injured people and grieving families to identify a defect, find a lawyer, and file.

It restricts punitive damages, including limiting evidence that can be used solely to support a punitive award, and directs courts to strictly enforce Rule 11 sanctions — orders that can force losing plaintiffs to pay the other side's legal fees — which raises the risk of suing.

It gives federal district courts jurisdiction over these cases and lets federal judges transfer them between districts, moving most claims out of state courts where juries had historically been more receptive to crash victims.

analysis.who_pays: Victims of small-plane crashes and their families. Anyone hurt by a defective aircraft or part delivered more than 20 years earlier would have had no claim against the manufacturer, even if a hidden defect caused the crash, and all victims would have had only two years to sue, faced limits on punitive damages, and could be ordered to pay a manufacturer's legal fees if a case were deemed frivolous. States would also lose their authority to set safety-liability rules for accidents on their own soil.
analysis.who_pays_short: Crash victims, families, and state courts

drawbacks.text: A 20-year cutoff from delivery would bar suits over aircraft that are decades old even when a hidden defect is discovered later — and small planes often stay in service for 30 years or more, so victims of the oldest aircraft would have no recourse at all.
A two-year filing window after an accident is very short for crash victims and families, who must first determine what part failed and who made it before they can even file.

Strictly enforced Rule 11 sanctions, including orders to pay the other party's legal fees, would raise the cost and risk of bringing claims, discouraging cases with uncertain facts from ever being filed.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill's rationale: liability exposure for decades-old aircraft was widely cited as a reason small-plane makers struggled with insurance costs and, in some cases, curtailed production during the 1980s, and shielding manufacturers was presented as a way to keep the industry — and the aircraft owners who depend on it — in business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a large, permanent reduction in legal liability to one concentrated industry while putting the entire cost of plane-crash injuries on the victims themselves — particularly those harmed by aircraft already more than 20 years old, who would have received nothing. The industry's insurance-cost argument had real force, but the bill's remedy was not to share that cost with aircraft owners or to improve safety; it was to eliminate the victims' claims, and to do so for every state at once through federal preemption. A bill that addressed the insurance problem while preserving compensation for victims whose planes failed through hidden defects would have balanced the interests better.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee — it got one hearing in September 1991 but the committee never voted to send it to the Senate floor, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum (R-KS) introduced the bill on March 13, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill attracted 26 cosponsors — 21 Republicans and 5 Democrats — a broadly bipartisan slate of support.
The Commerce Committee held a hearing on the bill on September 19, 1991, its only recorded action beyond referral.
The committee never reported the bill to the Senate, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died on January 3, 1993, when the 102nd Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crash victims and their families, who kept their existing right to sue small-aircraft manufacturers under state law without the 20-year cutoff or two-year filing window this bill would have imposed. Manufacturers, who stood to gain the most from the liability limits, gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crash victims who kept their right to sue

for.name: Nancy Landon Kassebaum
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 13, 1991, and championed federal liability limits for general aviation manufacturers in her home state's major industry.

for.name: General Aviation Manufacturers Association
for.what_they_did: Backed federal legislation to cap liability for aircraft delivered years earlier, the industry's central legislative priority of that period.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Held a single hearing on September 19, 1991, but never marked the bill up or reported it to the Senate floor, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal liability limits of this kind, which would bar suits against manufacturers over older aircraft and cap the damages their clients could recover.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 21 Republicans and 5 Democrats signed on — but the bill sat in a Democratic-chaired committee and never reached the floor, so no vote ever tested the parties' positions.

industries.note: The bill would have shielded makers of small planes and parts from suits over aircraft delivered more than 20 years earlier and from most punitive damages — a direct reduction in their largest recurring legal cost, paid for by eliminating crash victims' claims.
Capping manufacturers' exposure to lawsuits over older planes would have sharply reduced the insurers' payouts and premiums priced around open-ended liability.

A 20-year repose, a two-year filing window, and enforceable fee-shifting sanctions would have eliminated many contingency-fee cases against manufacturers; the lawyers' financial interest in this bill ran alongside their clients' interest in keeping claims open.
